title: Immigrants Founded 59 Percent Of America's Billion-Dollar Startups
excerpt: A new NFAP analysis of 775 US unicorn companies finds immigrants founded or co-founded 455 of them, worth a collective $5 trillion. India leads all nations with 96 billion-dollar companies traced to Indian-born entrepreneurs.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Immigrants founded 59% of US unicorns, valued at $5 trillion, up from 55% in 2018.
  • India leads with 96 billion-dollar startups, followed by Israel (60) and the UK (47).
  • 24% of US unicorns have founders who arrived as international students.
  • 46.2% of Fortune 500 companies were founded by immigrants, generating $8.6 trillion in revenue.

National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP)
  • Immigrants founded or co-founded 59% of all 775 US unicorn companies, up from 55% in 2018, with a collective valuation of $5 trillion.
  • India leads all nations with 96 billion-dollar startups, followed by Israel (60), the United Kingdom (47) and China (41).
  • Nearly one in four US unicorn companies were founded by individuals who first came to the United States as international students.
  • 46.2% of Fortune 500 companies were also founded by immigrants or their children, generating $8.6 trillion in annual revenue.

Immigrants have founded or co-founded 455 of America's 775 privately held billion-dollar startup companies, accounting for 59% of the country's unicorn economy and representing a collective valuation of $5 trillion, according to an April 2026 analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

The figure marks a steady increase from the 55% recorded in NFAP's 2018 and 2022 reports. When the children of immigrants are included, two-thirds of all US billion-dollar companies trace their origins to foreign-born founders or their immediate descendants. Close to 80% have an immigrant in a key leadership role such as chief executive or vice president of engineering.

India Leads the Pack by a Wide Margin

India sits at the top of the rankings with 96 billion-dollar companies traced to Indian-born entrepreneurs — far ahead of the nearest competitors. Israel follows with 60, the United Kingdom with 47, China with 41, Canada with 30, Russia with 23 and France with 21. In total, immigrant entrepreneurs from 76 countries have contributed to founding US unicorn companies.

Among the highest-valued companies with immigrant founders are SpaceX ($1.5 trillion), Anthropic ($965 billion), OpenAI ($852 billion), Databricks ($134 billion) and Stripe ($106.7 billion).

"U.S. billion-dollar companies with immigrant founders represent America's cutting-edge companies in AI, medical research, space, defense, healthcare, cybersecurity, enterprise management and other fields."

- National Foundation for American Policy report

Indian Founders Building Multi-Billion-Dollar Fortunes

The wealthiest Indian immigrant founders of US unicorns underscore the scale of the diaspora's contribution. Jay Chaudhry, who grew up in the small town of Panoh in Himachal Pradesh — a village without running water or electricity — founded cybersecurity firm Zscaler and holds a net worth of $13.1 billion, according to Forbes 2025 data.

Vinod Khosla, co-founder of Sun Microsystems and founder of Khosla Ventures, follows at $9.2 billion. Rakesh Gangwal, co-founder of IndiGo and former chairman of US Airways Group, holds $6.6 billion. Romesh Wadhwani, founder of Symphony Technology Group, has $5 billion, and Aneel Bhusri, co-founder of Workday, rounds out the top five at $3.3 billion.

Six of the 15 immigrants who have founded two or more billion-dollar companies are Indian: Mohit Aron, Jyoti Bansal, Ashutosh Garg, Arvind Jain, Sachin Nayyar and Ajeet Singh.

The International Student Pipeline

The NFAP research highlights international students as a disproportionate driver of unicorn creation. Some 183 of 775 US billion-dollar companies — 24% — have at least one founder who first arrived in the United States on a student visa. Those companies employ an average of 1,123 people each and carry a combined valuation between $3.5 trillion and $4 trillion.

At American universities, international students account for 80% of full-time graduate enrolments in computer and information sciences, 75% in electrical and computer engineering and 62% in mathematics and statistics — fields that feed directly into startup creation.

The Association of American Universities noted that these findings arrive as US immigration policies grow more restrictive. International students now face longer visa processing times, social media vetting and an oversubscribed H-1B lottery, with recent changes further reducing the odds for new graduates.

Fortune 500 Data Reinforces the Pattern

A separate August 2025 analysis by the American Immigration Council found that 46.2% of Fortune 500 companies (231 of 500) were founded by immigrants or their children — the highest level since tracking began in 2011. These companies generated $8.6 trillion in revenue in fiscal year 2024 and employed over 15.4 million people worldwide.

Among the 14 companies appearing on the Fortune 500 list for the first time that year, 10 were founded by immigrants or their children. The companies span industries from technology to retail to media, including Amazon, Apple, NVIDIA and Levi Strauss.

What Comes Next

The NFAP concluded that without immigrant founders, the United States would likely have fewer than half as many billion-dollar companies, hundreds of thousands fewer jobs and up to $5 trillion less in wealth. As immigration policy debates intensify, the data presents a stark economic case for the channels through which these entrepreneurs have historically entered and remained in the country.

For the Indian diaspora — the single largest source of unicorn founders — the stakes are particularly high. Any narrowing of student visa pathways or work permit programs would disproportionately affect the pipeline that has produced 96 billion-dollar companies and counting.
